definition.text: The point at which a fairly small change in outside conditions sets off a rapid change in an ecosystem.

facts.text: Once a threshold is passed, the ecosystem may not be able to return to its earlier state through its own resilience.
Thresholds show that ecosystems respond non-linearly to pressures from human activity or natural processes.
Thresholds can be sharp points or zones in which the shift from one state to another is gradual.
Many crossed thresholds have proved hard or nearly impossible to undo, which is why they are called points of no return; extinction is a definitive example.
Thresholds often show hysteresis: the way back from the altered state can be very different from the path that led there.
Detecting a threshold is not always easy; one approach scans time series for a sudden jump.
Clear lakes turning turbid is a well documented example, and a database by the Resilience Alliance and Santa Fe Institute lists over one hundred cases.
Critical load, regime shift, critical transition and tipping point are closely related terms.

definition.text: The largest population of a species that a particular environment can keep going over time, given its food, habitat, water and other resources.

facts.text: At carrying capacity, births equal deaths (plus immigration and emigration), so the population is in equilibrium.
Below carrying capacity a population can grow; above it, the population usually shrinks for lack of space, food or sunlight.
The factor that stops a population growing, such as food, water, nesting space or the waste the environment can absorb, is called a limiting factor.
Applied to an environment as a whole, carrying capacity means resources are not taken faster than they regrow and wastes stay within what nature can absorb.
The idea is used to find the maximum population an environment can support in ecology, agriculture and fisheries.
The term spread through biology in the 1870s, was developed in wildlife and livestock management in the early 1900s and became a staple of ecology by the 1950s.
Many authors doubt its usefulness for wild populations, since it can oversimplify how species interact.

definition.text: A population model in which growth slows as numbers approach the carrying capacity K and stops at K.

facts.text: Verhulst's equation is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where N is population size, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K the carrying capacity.
When the population is small it grows exponentially; as it nears K, growth falls and reaches zero.
Solving the equation gives the S-shaped logistic growth curve N(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(−rt)).
The letter K comes from the German Kapazitätsgrenze, meaning capacity limit.
Pierre François Verhulst published the equations in 1838 without using the term carrying capacity.

definition.text: In farming, the number of livestock a piece of land can carry, used to set a sustainable stocking rate.

facts.text: Hadwen and Palmer (1923) defined carrying capacity as the density of stock that could graze for a set period without damaging the range.
In Australia paddock capacity is counted in Dry Sheep Equivalents; one DSE is a 50 kg Merino wether or dry ewe kept in stable condition.
Other countries use other units; the United Kingdom measures paddocks in livestock units.

title: Human carrying capacity

definition.text: The number of people the Earth or a region can support, which depends on how people live and the technology they use.

facts.text: The agricultural and industrial revolutions raised human carrying capacity, letting population grow from 5 to 10 million in 10,000 BCE to 1.5 billion in 1900.
Without the Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people.
These successes have come at grave environmental cost, including climate change, ocean acidification and dead zones at river mouths.
Degrading the ecosystem services people depend on could lower Earth's human carrying capacity; some argue 8 billion may already be above it.
Measuring it is arbitrary: choices about what counts as food or water, and the fact that regions trade resources, change the answer.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005, involving more than 1,300 experts, warned that rapid ecosystem change threatens long-term human carrying capacity.
Crossing one planetary boundary does not prove carrying capacity is exceeded, but crossing several makes that harder to deny.
A 2004 meta-analysis of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion people, with bounds of 0.65 and 98 billion.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether today's human population already exceeds Earth's long-run carrying capacity and how far technology can raise it.

definition.text: A framework that sets limits on how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself.

facts.text: Crossing the limits could push the Earth system out of the stable Holocene period in which human society developed.

The nine boundaries are climate change, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading.
Its authors warned that transgressing boundaries risks crossing thresholds that trigger non-linear, abrupt change at continental to planetary scale.
The framework was developed in 2009 by scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University.
In 2009 three boundaries were judged crossed; the 2015 update found four crossed.
Novel entities were judged the 5th transgressed boundary in 2022, freshwater change the 6th in 2023 and ocean acidification the 7th in 2025.
Agriculture and food contribute to the transgression of four of the nine boundaries, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows most important.
UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012, though it was later dropped from the Rio+20 text over poorer countries' worries about sidelining development.

definition.text: The measurable quantities and limit values the framework uses to track how far humanity has shifted the Earth away from Holocene conditions.

facts.text: The 2009 study quantified seven of the nine boundaries; by 2025 eight were quantified.
The climate boundary is 350 ppm of atmospheric CO2, against a current 423 ppm and a pre-industrial 280 ppm.
The biosphere integrity boundary is under 10 extinctions per million species-years, while the current rate is over 100.
The land system boundary keeps 75% of forests intact; the global figure is 59%.
Industrial and intentional nitrogen fixation has a boundary of 62 Tg per year against a current 165 Tg per year.
Aerosol loading and stratospheric ozone depletion are the two boundaries listed as not exceeded.
For several processes no single threshold point can be located, because the Earth system is complex and evidence is still partial.

definition.text: The zone inside the planetary boundaries where Holocene-like conditions can be kept and risks to societies stay low.

facts.text: Each control variable has a range of values; the boundary is set at the lower end of that range.
Beyond the range lies a poorly predictable world, and persistent crossing pushes the world further into a danger zone.
The authors framed boundaries as a safe space for human development, an advance on simply minimising human impact.

definition.text: The ways that pushing one planetary boundary changes the safe level of others.

facts.text: The authors suggested a crossed boundary shrinks the safe operating space for other processes rather than enlarging it.
For example, breaching the freshwater boundary could make land arid and lower the land-use boundary.
Warming, acidity and UV together stress marine life far more than any single stressor alone.

definition.text: The healthy functioning of Earth's life-support systems, also called ecological integrity.

facts.text: Scholars say planetary integrity must be maintained for long-term sustainability.

title: Critiques of planetary boundaries

definition.text: The arguments over whether fixed global limits are a fair and useful guide for environmental policy.

facts.text: Development scholars argue forest-conservation targets reward rich countries that already cleared their forests while asking poorer ones to sacrifice.
William Schlesinger warns that managing to a threshold lets slow, diffuse degradation persist almost indefinitely.
Critics note the framework treats the Holocene as a safe zone even though it never involved industrial farming.
Supporters say it highlights the risk of abrupt, non-linear change and can help build agreements on threats such as climate change.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether planetary boundaries are fair to the Global South and whether threshold-based management works.

definition.text: The capacity of an ecosystem to resist damage from a disturbance and then recover.

facts.text: Disturbances include fires, floods, windstorms and insect outbreaks, as well as human acts such as deforestation, pesticide use and introducing exotic species.
A large or long enough disturbance can push an ecosystem past a threshold into a different regime of processes and structures.
Biodiversity loss, resource exploitation, pollution, land use and climate change increasingly cause regime shifts, often to degraded states.
Canadian ecologist C.S. Holling first introduced the idea to describe how natural systems persist through change.
The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report counts the capacity for transformation as part of resilience, alongside keeping function, identity and structure.
A forest can usually recover from damage such as lightning or landslides affecting up to 10 percent of its area; larger damage makes recovery harder.
Sustainable use of environmental goods and services requires understanding an ecosystem's resilience and its limits.
Interest has shifted from the maximum sustainable yield paradigm toward ecosystem management that builds resilience through adaptive management and governance.

definition.text: Two meanings of resilience: how fast a system returns to equilibrium after a shock, versus how much disturbance it can absorb while keeping the same function and structure.

facts.text: Holling called the return-time meaning 'engineering resilience' because physics and engineering use it.
Ecological resilience assumes a system can exist in multiple stable states or regimes.
Some shallow lakes can sit in a clear-water regime rich in ecosystem services or a turbid regime with fewer services and toxic algae blooms, depending on phosphorus.
Australia's Mulga woodlands can be grass-rich and good for sheep or shrub-dominated and useless for grazing, driven by fire, herbivory and rainfall.

definition.text: Brian Walker, C.S. Holling and others break resilience into latitude, resistance, precariousness and panarchy.

facts.text: Latitude is how far a system can be changed before it loses the ability to recover.
Resistance is how hard the system is to change, and precariousness is how close it currently sits to a threshold.
Panarchy is how much one level of an ecosystem's hierarchy is influenced by the other levels.
Adaptive capacity, closely linked to resilience, is people's ability to cope with environmental change by observing, learning and altering their interactions.

title: Resilience versus market specialisation
article: Ecological resilience#The flaw of the free market

definition.text: The argument that free-market efficiency, which depends on specialisation, weakens the resilience of social and ecological systems.

facts.text: Applying ecological resilience to sustainable development sits at odds with conventional economic ideology and policy.
Specialisation makes systems accustomed to and dependent on prevailing conditions, which lowers their resilience.
Andrea Ross argues sustainable development rests on weak sustainability and ignores limits to Earth's resilience.

contested_note: Resilience thinking questions the free-market model that conventional economic policy relies on.

title: Tipping points in the climate system
article: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: A critical threshold in the climate system that, once crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible change.

facts.text: The IPCC defines a tipping point as a threshold beyond which a system reorganises, often abruptly or irreversibly.
A small disturbance can cause a disproportionately large change, often through self-reinforcing feedbacks.
Tipping behaviour appears in ice sheets, glaciers, ocean circulation, ecosystems and the atmosphere.
Thawing permafrost releasing methane and melting ice lowering Earth's albedo are examples that would speed warming.
Early IPCC work thought tipping likely only above 4 °C of warming; by 2021 tipping was considered significantly probable at just over 1 °C and highly probable above 2 °C.
Crossing tipping points would likely have severe impacts on human society and could accelerate global warming.

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Climate tipping elements
article: Tipping points in the climate system#Comparison of tipping points

definition.text: The parts of the climate system, such as ice sheets, ocean currents and large forests, that may have tipping points.

facts.text: As of September 2022, nine global core tipping elements and seven regional impact tipping elements had been identified.
Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheet collapse, tropical coral reef die-off and abrupt boreal permafrost thaw are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming.
Completely melting the Greenland ice sheet would raise global sea levels by 7.2 metres.
A collapse of the Atlantic overturning circulation would cool parts of Europe by over 10 °C and threaten crop yields across most world regions.
Around 500 million people depend on coral reefs, and a sustained ocean temperature rise of 1 °C above average is enough to cause bleaching.
Permafrost holds carbon from organisms that died over thousands of years.

distinct_from: Tipping points in the climate system

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Amazon rainforest dieback
article: Tipping points in the climate system#Amazon rainforest dieback

definition.text: The risk that enough forest loss pushes much of the Amazon past a threshold into drier degraded forest or savanna.

facts.text: The Amazon makes around half of its own rainfall by recycling moisture, so forest loss means less rain downwind.
A 2022 study reported the rainforest has been losing resilience since the early 2000s, measured by slower recovery from short shocks.
Modelling suggests warming of 1.5–1.9°C combined with 22–28% deforestation could trigger a transition across 62–77% of the forest.
Some 17–18% of the Amazon has already been cleared for development.

distinct_from: Tipping points in the climate system

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Cascading tipping points
article: Tipping points in the climate system#Cascading tipping points

definition.text: A chain reaction in which crossing one climate threshold pushes another tipping element into a new state.

facts.text: Ice loss in Greenland and West Antarctica will alter ocean circulation and the two ice sheets likely destabilise each other.
In a 2021 study of three million simulations, nearly a third produced domino effects even with warming limited to 2 °C.
Temporarily overshooting Paris goals could raise the risk of tipping cascades by up to 72%.

distinct_from: Tipping points in the climate system

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Types of climate tipping
article: Tipping points in the climate system#Mathematical theory

definition.text: Three mathematical kinds of tipping: bifurcation-induced, noise-induced and rate-induced.

facts.text: Bifurcation-induced tipping happens when a parameter passes a critical level and a stable state loses stability or disappears.
Noise-induced tipping is caused by random fluctuations and gives no early warning, so it is unpredictable.
Rate-induced tipping occurs when the environment changes faster than the system can restore itself, as in peatland 'compost bomb' carbon release.

distinct_from: Tipping points in the climate system

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Hothouse Earth
article: Tipping points in the climate system#Potential impacts

definition.text: A proposed scenario in which crossing a warming threshold sets off tipping points and feedbacks that keep the climate from stabilising.

facts.text: Researchers proposed the threshold could lie around 2 °C above pre-industrial levels.
Such a state could raise sea levels by up to 60 metres and temperatures by 4–5 °C, above any interglacial in 1.2 million years.
The existence and value of the threshold remain speculative.

contested_note: Whether a Hothouse Earth threshold exists, and at what warming, is speculative.
distinct_from: Tipping points in the climate system

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

title: Regime shift

definition.text: A large, abrupt and lasting change in how an ecosystem, the climate, a financial system or another complex system is structured and works.

facts.text: A regime is a typical behaviour of a system held in place by mutually reinforcing feedbacks.
Shifts happen when stabilising feedbacks weaken or an external shock exceeds the system's capacity to absorb it.
Regime shifts matter in ecology because they can sharply change the flow of ecosystem services such as food, clean water and climate regulation.
They are hard to reverse and sometimes irreversible.
A small disturbance can produce big effects, so inputs and outputs are not proportional.
Regime shifts are expected to become more common as human influence on the planet grows.
Strong evidence emerged in the 1990s from kelp forests, coral reefs, drylands and shallow lakes.
Deforestation could shift Amazon and East Asian rainforests toward savanna, affecting food, fresh water, climate regulation and biodiversity.

contested_note: There is no agreed definition, and how the concept should be applied remains contested.

definition.text: Three patterns of change in systems prone to regime shifts, set by how fast and slow processes interact.

facts.text: Smooth change follows a nearly straight-line relationship between slow and fast variables; abrupt change follows a non-linear one.
In discontinuous change the system flips back at a different point from where it flipped forward, which is hysteresis.
Woody plant encroachment on drylands, where small changes in grazing shift grassland to woody savanna, is thought to be a smooth-change case.

title: Detecting regime shifts
article: Regime shift#Detection of whether a regime shift has occurred

definition.text: Statistical ways of telling from data whether a system has already shifted regime.

facts.text: Methods such as principal component analysis or neural networks need long data series and only work after the threshold is crossed.
Failing to find multiple regimes in data does not rule out a future shift.
For managers, assuming a system has only one regime can be risky when the alternatives are very harmful.

title: Alternative stable state

definition.text: The ecological theory that an ecosystem can settle into more than one stable state under the same conditions.

facts.text: A move between states, called a state shift, phase shift or regime shift, happens when the ecosystem is perturbed.
Feedbacks make ecosystems resist shifting, so they stay in one state unless the push is large enough.
Discrete states are separated by ecological thresholds, unlike ecosystems that change smoothly along a gradient.
Richard Lewontin first proposed the theory in 1969.
Coral reefs can flip from coral-dominated to degraded algae-dominated systems when algae grazers decline.
A 2005 review found 21 valid direct experiments, of which 14 supported alternative stable states and 8 did not.
If stable states exist, gradual change may have little effect until a threshold triggers a catastrophic shift, which matters for monitoring and restoration.

distinct_from: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

title: Ball-and-cup model

definition.text: A picture of ecosystem states as a ball rolling on a landscape of valleys and hills.

facts.text: In the simplest version two valleys are separated by a hill; a ball in a valley sits in a stable state, or domain of attraction.
Moving the ball to another valley takes enough force to push it over the hill.
A steep-sided valley is more resilient than a shallow one.

distinct_from: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

title: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

definition.text: Two explanations of state shifts: pushing fast-changing state variables directly, or changing slow parameters that reshape the landscape of states.

facts.text: State variables, such as population densities, respond quickly to system feedbacks; parameters respond slowly or not at all.
In the community view the landscape is fixed; in the ecosystem view environmental drivers change the number, location and resilience of stable states.

title: Human erosion of ecosystem resilience

definition.text: The ways human activity makes stable ecosystem states easier to tip into worse ones.

facts.text: People reduce resilience by cutting diversity (as in overfishing), altering the physical and chemical environment, and changing disturbance regimes such as through bottom trawling.
With less resilience, minor perturbations can push ecosystems into less desirable states.
Such shifts often lose ecosystem services and have been documented on land, at sea and in fresh water.

distinct_from: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

title: Balance of nature

definition.text: The idea that ecosystems naturally sit in a stable equilibrium, with small changes corrected by negative feedback.

facts.text: The idea is ancient: Herodotus, Plato and Cicero all described a balance in nature.
It once governed ecological research and natural resource management, and was a central theme of Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring.
Ecologists abandoned it in the late 20th century because constant disturbance and chaotic change turned out to be the norm.
An eight-year study of isolated Baltic plankton showed species populations rising and falling chaotically even under constant conditions.
Many habitats were shaped by people, such as Aboriginal fire-stick farming in Australia.
The idea remains popular with the public, conservationists and environmental groups.

contested_note: Ecologists have discredited the theory, yet some still call it a foundational metaphor and it stays popular with the public.

definition.text: A system made of many interacting parts that adapt and learn, whose overall behaviour cannot be predicted from the parts alone.

facts.text: Examples include climate, cities, firms, markets, governments, ecosystems, power grids and ant colonies.
Interactions are non-linear, so small changes in inputs can cause large changes in outputs, and any interaction can feed back on itself.
Such systems often organise themselves rather than following a central hierarchy.
Their high adaptive capacity gives them resilience against disturbance.
They run far from equilibrium and need a constant flow of energy to keep their organisation.
Sociologist Walter F. Buckley coined the term in 1968.
The approach is increasingly used to study economic development and institutional change, where outcomes can be influenced but not precisely controlled.
They are often modelled with agent-based and network models.

definition.text: A view of human systems (economic, social, cultural) and natural systems (water, air, living things, rocks) as linked by two-way interactions.

facts.text: The idea is that human and environmental systems can no longer be studied as separate, isolated systems.
Research frameworks track flows of information, energy, materials, organisms, people and capital between systems, and the agents whose decisions shape them.
Integrated studies reveal feedback loops, non-linearity, thresholds, surprises and legacy effects with time lags that single-discipline work hides.
A foundational study in Wolong Nature Reserve, China, found that subsidies for guarding forests and converting farmland to forest improved panda habitat.
The phrase appears in literature from 1999, and the US National Science Foundation made it a standing research program in 2007.
It builds on social-ecological system theory but covers all aspects of human and natural life, not only social and environmental ones.

definition.text: Interactions between coupled human and natural systems that are far apart, one of four scales in coupled-systems research.

facts.text: Intracoupling studies one coupled system, pericoupling two neighbouring systems, telecoupling two distant ones, and metacoupling all three at once.
A sending system passes a flow to a receiving system, and a spillover system is affected without being the focus.

definition.text: A change in environmental conditions that causes a marked change in an ecosystem.

facts.text: Disturbances include fires, floods, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions.
They range in scale from a single tree falling to a mass extinction.
Many ecosystems are maintained by regular disturbance; wetlands, for example, by moving water and periodic fires.
Right after a disturbance there is a pulse of regrowth because competition for space and resources is low.
Biological diversity depends on natural disturbance; many shade-intolerant plants need it to establish.
In western US ponderosa pine forests, suppressing surface fires lets dense Douglas fir take over, cutting light, plant diversity and the animals that rely on them.
How species cope with disturbance may predict their ability to adapt to climate change.

definition.text: Disturbance to ecosystems caused by human activity.

facts.text: Logging, dredging, converting land to ranching or farming, mowing and mining are examples.
Human disturbance worldwide has spread disturbance-adapted species, often called weeds.
Controlled burns by Native Americans maintained fire-dependent ecosystems and helped keep them stable and diverse.
Human-caused climate change is considered a major force shaping future ecosystem change.

definition.text: Repeating patterns in which disturbance, regrowth and succession set an ecosystem up for the next disturbance.

facts.text: Without further disturbance, many ecosystems drift back toward pre-disturbance conditions through ecological succession.
Mountain pine beetle outbreaks in western North America kill old pines, opening gaps where other trees thrive until pines regrow.
In 2004 the beetles affected more than 90,000 square kilometres.

definition.text: Pioneer or early successional species that quickly exploit freshly disturbed sites.

facts.text: Fast-growing, shade-intolerant species such as pin cherry and aspen fill gaps left by fire or windstorms.
Jack pine has serotinous cones that open only with the heat of fire.

title: Ecological stability

definition.text: An ecosystem's ability to return to equilibrium after a disturbance, or to avoid sudden large changes over time.

facts.text: An ecosystem can be stable in some properties and not others; a plant community in drought may keep its biomass but lose biodiversity.
In 1997 Grimm and Wissel counted 167 definitions in the literature covering 70 different stability concepts.
They proposed replacing the term with more specific ones such as constancy, resilience and persistence.
Not every ecosystem is stable, as with wolves and moose on Isle Royale.
The concept emerged in the first half of the 20th century and spread with theoretical ecology in the 1970s.

contested_note: Overuse of the term has led to controversy over how ecological stability should be defined.

definition.text: The separate kinds of stability ecologists measure, such as constancy, resistance, persistence and resilience.

facts.text: Resistance measures how little a variable changes under outside pressure; inertia or persistence is the ability to resist fluctuations.
Resilience is the tendency to keep structure and recover after disturbance; elasticity is how fast it returns and amplitude how far it can be moved and still return.
Local stability covers small, short disturbances; global stability means strong resistance to change in species composition or food webs.

title: May stability criterion
article: Ecological stability#May stability analysis and random matrix theory

definition.text: Robert May's result that a large random ecosystem loses stability once its species number and interaction strength pass a limit.

facts.text: May linearised the species equations around equilibrium using the Jacobian, also called the community matrix.
Treating the Jacobian as a random matrix, the system loses stability when S exceeds 1/σ, where σ is the spread of interaction strengths.
The result implies diversity limits dynamical stability.

title: Diversity–stability debate

definition.text: The long-running question of whether more diverse ecosystems are more stable.

facts.text: Charles Elton argued in 1958 that complex, diverse communities tend to be more stable; Robert May later refuted the idea that diversity begets stability.
Diversity can stabilise ecosystem functions; genetic diversity, for example, can improve resistance to disturbance.
In food-web models the effect of diversity on stability can be positive or negative, depending on network structure.

contested_note: Elton held that diversity brings stability while May's models showed it can limit stability; evidence points both ways.

title: Ecosystem collapse

definition.text: The loss of an ecosystem's defining features and the services it provided once destabilising pressures push it past a critical threshold.

facts.text: Collapse does not mean all life disappears; the original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function.
It has been called an analogue of species extinction and is usually irreversible; any recovery is slow and needs active intervention.
Human drivers include introducing species, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and habitat destruction or fragmentation.
Collapse can occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biotic processes.
Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves, against 84% now.
Under a high-emissions scenario, tropical ocean ecosystems could face abrupt disruption before 2030, with tropical forests and polar regions following by 2050.
Little is known yet about effective ways to conserve or reverse collapsing ecosystems.

notes: The dossier's Definition line (S:acce03c90953) defines 'ecosystem', not collapse; the definition uses lead sentences instead.

definition.text: Documented cases in which ecosystems collapsed through overuse, climate shocks or introduced species.

facts.text: Easter Island's palm-dominated forests collapsed from overexploitation, climate change and introduced rats.
The Aral Sea shrank after its feeder rivers were diverted for irrigation, falling to 10% of its original size by 1997.
Overfishing reduced Grand Banks cod to 1% of historical levels in the early 1990s.
In the northern Benguela upwelling, overfishing and climate events turned a sardine-dominated ecosystem into one dominated by jellyfish and goby.

definition.text: Tools such as risk assessment protocols and simulation models that estimate how close ecosystems are to collapse.

facts.text: The IUCN Red List of Ecosystems is a global standard that works even where data are scarce.
It uses Collapsed as the end-point category, with Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered defined by the risk of collapse.
Because it compares systems to a criteria list, it is often paired with simulation models covering dynamics, future threats and social links.

title: Ecosystem health

definition.text: A metaphor for the overall condition of an ecosystem.

facts.text: Fire, drought, invasive species, climate change, mining, fishing, farming and logging can all change ecosystem condition.
There is no universal benchmark; judgements depend on the metrics chosen and the goals of society.
Supporters value it as a simple communication tool, while critics call it a value-laden idea passed off as science.
Aldo Leopold spoke of land health and land sickness; the health metaphor dates back at least to the early 1800s.
The Great Lakes Basin uses a suite of 80 lake health indicators, including native fish, phosphorus and toxic chemicals.
A healthy state is hard to pin down because species in an ecosystem reshuffle over time.
Proposed neutral alternatives include ecosystem status, ecosystem prognosis and ecosystem sustainability.

contested_note: Critics argue ecosystem health is a value judgement rather than a scientific measure.

definition.text: The difference between indicators used to describe trends scientifically and those used to rank conditions as good or bad for policy.

facts.text: An indicator is a measured variable used to infer trends in something unmeasured; rising chlorophyll-a in a lake may signal eutrophication.
The same chlorophyll level may be judged healthy in a natural wetland and unhealthy in a human-impacted one.
Critics say mixing the two implies values can be measured objectively, and urge keeping them separate.

title: Health paradox
article: Ecosystem health#Relationship to human health: the health paradox

definition.text: The trade-off in which human health has often improved by sacrificing the health of wild ecosystems.

facts.text: Examples include damming valleys, draining mosquito-bearing wetlands, diverting water for irrigation and converting wilderness to farmland.
The utilitarian view treats human well-being as a test of ecosystem health; the protectionist view sees humans as an invasive species.
Utilitarians argue unhealthy ecosystems bring more disease, fires, floods, crop failures and fishery collapse.

contested_note: Conservationists and resource managers are split over whether to scale back or embrace human domination of the biosphere.

definition.text: What happens when a system's outputs loop back to become its inputs, forming a circuit of cause and effect.

facts.text: Because each part influences the other, simple cause-and-effect reasoning fails and the system must be analysed as a whole.
The first known artificial feedback device was a float valve for keeping water at a constant level, invented in 270 BC in Alexandria.
The idea entered economic theory in Britain by the 18th century, though it did not yet have a name.
In organisms, ecosystems and the biosphere, most parameters must be held within a narrow range around an optimal level.
The climate system has strong positive and negative feedback loops linking atmosphere, ocean and land.
Many systems with several loops cannot be classed simply as positive or negative feedback.

definition.text: Feedback that amplifies a change (positive, or reinforcing) versus feedback that counteracts it (negative, or balancing).

facts.text: Positive feedback widens the gap between a target and the actual value; negative feedback narrows it.
Other names are self-reinforcing and self-correcting, or reinforcing and balancing.
A car's cruise control, which holds a target speed, is an example of negative feedback.
Melting snow exposes darker ground that absorbs more heat and melts more snow: the ice–albedo positive feedback.
Negative feedback is often added deliberately to make a system more stable and accurate.

definition.text: When the state of a system depends on its history, not just on present conditions.

facts.text: Plots often form a hysteresis loop, with different values of one variable depending on which way another variable is changing.
Sir James Alfred Ewing coined the term in 1881, from a Greek word meaning 'lagging behind'.
In ecology, a system's equilibrium cannot be predicted from environmental variables alone; its past matters too, as with spruce budworm outbreaks.
A thermostat that turns heat on below 18 °C but off only above 22 °C uses hysteresis deliberately.
Agar melts at 85 °C but solidifies only at 32 to 40 °C.

definition.text: The idea that a temporary economic shock can leave lasting effects, such as permanently higher unemployment.

facts.text: Starting exports may need a big push because of fixed transport costs, but once begun little is needed to keep them going.
In recessions unemployed workers may lose skills or motivation and stay jobless during the recovery.
Olivier Blanchard and others used hysteresis to explain long-run unemployment differences between Europe and the United States.

definition.text: When a population grows beyond its local carrying capacity, using resources faster than they can be replaced.

facts.text: Overshoot can lead to a crash if resources are depleted faster than they regenerate; the path is called overshoot-and-collapse.
It can happen because of delayed impacts, when births keep exceeding deaths.
On St. Matthew Island, 29 reindeer introduced in 1944 grew to about 6000 by 1963, then crashed to 42 by 1965.
In the Horn of Africa, after smallpox was eradicated, a pastoralist population of about 1 million grew to 14 million, causing overgrazing and soil erosion.
Prolonged overshoot can profoundly change and simplify entire ecosystems.

title: Human overshoot

definition.text: The share of human demand on nature, driven by both consumption and population, that exceeds what Earth can sustainably supply.

facts.text: The 1972 Limits to Growth model projected a carrying capacity of ten to fourteen billion people followed by collapse; economists generally dismissed it.
William R. Catton Jr.'s 1980 book Overshoot blamed both overpopulation and overconsumption.
Humanity's consumption relative to Earth's regenerative capacity rose from 73% in 1960 to 170% in 2016, especially in richer countries.
Fossil fuels have let human demand detach from the limits of biological regeneration.
Fossil fuels supply 85% of commercial energy and 65% of fibre production.
Overshoot has been discussed as a cause of societal collapse but has not been found to have caused historic collapses.

contested_note: How far humanity is in overshoot, and whether population or consumption is the main driver, is debated.

title: Neo-Malthusian scarcity debate

definition.text: The argument over whether population growth will outrun food and resources, as Malthus and later Ehrlich predicted.

facts.text: Malthus forecast in 1798 that population growth would deplete the world's food; Ehrlich revived the argument in 1968.
Economist Julian Simon countered that the Green Revolution prevented famine; grain production rose over 250% between 1950 and 1984.
Neo-Malthusians reply that the Green Revolution depends on fossil-fuel fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation.
The FAO said in 2009 that the world would need 70% more food by 2050.

contested_note: Neo-Malthusians and economists such as Julian Simon disagree on whether technology can keep resources ahead of population.

definition.text: The field and movement studying how human health depends on the state of Earth's natural systems.

facts.text: It explores the consequences of environmental change for human health.
The Rockefeller Foundation–Lancet Commission launched the concept in 2015.
A guiding principle is that human health depends on flourishing natural systems and wise stewardship of them.
Its education framework has five domains, including interconnection with nature, equity and social justice, and systems thinking.
UNEP's 2025 GEO-7 report found that investing in planetary health could add trillions to global GDP and avoid millions of deaths.
An international commission created the planetary health diet in January 2019.

definition.text: The ability of a community or population to stay essentially unchanged when disturbed.

facts.text: Its opposite is sensitivity: sensitive species or communities change a lot under stress.
Grimm and Wissel reduced the many stability definitions to three core properties: staying unchanged, returning after disturbance, and persisting over time.
Some authors treat resistance as part of resilience rather than separate from it.
After Hurricane Joan in 1988, Qualea paraensis resisted with low mortality, while Vochysia ferruginea died heavily but recovered through seedlings.

conflicts.text: Grimm and Wissel found 70 terms and 163 distinct definitions of stability.
conflicts.note: Ecological stability page gives 167 definitions and 70 concepts (S:fd3abb118a75) for the same 1997 inventory.

definition.text: The properties of an ecosystem that limit how well introduced species can invade it.

facts.text: Charles Elton applied the term to these properties.
They include temperature and drought as well as competition, parasitism, predation and missing mutualists.
Higher species diversity and lower resource availability can add resistance.

definition.text: A unit of land, water and living things together with the people, organisations and institutions that use and govern it.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that humans are part of nature, so the line between social and ecological systems is artificial.
Berkes and Folke first put forward the idea.
Social and ecological parts are linked through feedbacks, and both show resilience and complexity.
Such systems are complex and adaptive and are bounded around particular ecosystems and their problems.
Non-linearity creates path dependency, multiple basins of attraction and the potential for threshold shifts.
Because subsystems nest within larger ones, complex systems should be analysed and managed at several scales at once.
Communities that interact with an ecosystem over long periods often hold the most relevant knowledge of its dynamics.

definition.text: Elinor Ostrom's framework for analysing social-ecological systems, built on the theory of common-pool resources and collective self-governance.

facts.text: It draws heavily on systems ecology and complexity theory.
Unlike complex adaptive systems theory, it includes concerns such as equity and human wellbeing.
It borrows from island biogeography, optimal foraging theory and microeconomic theory but is broader than any of them.

definition.text: Holling's model of how complex systems move through phases of growth, conservation, release and reorganisation.

facts.text: The cycle moves slowly from exploitation (r) to conservation (K), then rapidly to release (Omega) and reorganisation (alpha) before returning to exploitation.
After a cycle the system can begin anew or transform into a new configuration.
Connectedness and potential are the two dimensions that change across the four phases.
Adaptability is a system's capacity to learn and adjust; transformability is its capacity to become a completely new system; both underpin resilience.

definition.text: Governing social-ecological systems so that institutions can learn and reorganise as ecosystems change.

facts.text: Folke and colleagues contrasted the Florida Everglades and the Grand Canyon, both of which suffered degraded ecosystem services.
In the Everglades, conflict between farming and conservation interests left few feedbacks and little capacity to adapt.
At the Grand Canyon, an adaptive management workgroup used planned interventions and monitoring to learn, enabling successful reorganisation.
Introduced by Holling in 1978, it is a flexible approach to climate impacts that contrasts with mitigation-focused efforts.

definition.text: A way of understanding complexity by looking at wholes and the relationships between parts rather than breaking things into pieces.

facts.text: It is used to find effective action in complex situations and to bring about systems change.
A system is a set of interconnected things that produce their own pattern of behaviour over time.
Ludwig von Bertalanffy and Jay Forrester were early contributors, and Peter Senge's The Fifth Discipline popularised it in the 1990s.
Donella Meadows described leverage points: places where a small change can produce a large shift in behaviour.
Its methods include system dynamics, which models stocks, flows and internal feedback loops.
Ecological economics criticises the externality concept for lacking systems thinking.

definition.text: The interdisciplinary study of how humans relate to their natural, social and built environments.

facts.text: It emerged from ecology and the social sciences in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
It examines how populations adapt to environments and how technology and economies shape sustainability.
The land needed to sustain an urban region is typically at least an order of magnitude larger than the area within its boundaries.

title: Critical slowing down

definition.text: The increasingly slow recovery from small disturbances shown by a system approaching a tipping point, used as an early warning signal.

facts.text: As recovery slows, the system's autocorrelation and variance rise, giving measurable warning signs.
Since the early 2000s, more than three-quarters of the Amazon rainforest has shown slower recovery from short-term shocks, suggesting it may be nearing a critical transition.
Rising autocorrelation and variance in melt rates suggest the Greenland ice sheet is losing resilience.
Early warnings need long, good-quality data series, which are rare in ecology.
Noise-induced transitions give no such warning, and human-driven change may be too fast for signals to appear.

contested_note: It is unclear how well early warning signals work for all regime shifts and whether they give enough time to act.

sources.title: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: A view of linked human and natural systems as a nested set of adaptive cycles operating across different scales of time and space.

facts.text: In resilience theory, panarchy is how much one hierarchical level of an ecosystem is influenced by other levels.
C.S. Holling developed the idea, leading to the 2002 book Panarchy: understanding transformations in human and natural systems.
Panarchy and adaptive cycles have become an important lens for describing the resilience of ecological and social-ecological systems.
Though rooted in ecology, it is used in other fields, for example linking planetary, political-economic and supply-chain levels.
